claim: Vascular endothelial cell (EC) function depends on appropriate organ-specific molecular and cellular specializations.
source: Vascular endothelial cell (EC) function depends on appropriate organ-specific molecular and cellular specializations.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that sets up the study's rationale.

claim: The study analyzed and compared the transcriptome, accessible chromatin, and DNA methylome landscapes from mouse brain, liver, lung, and kidney ECs.
source: To explore genomic mechanisms that control this specialization, we have analyzed and compared the transcriptome, accessible chromatin, and DNA methylome landscapes from mouse brain, liver, lung, and kidney ECs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Analysis of transcription factor (TF) gene expression and TF motifs at candidate cis-regulatory elements reveals both shared and organ-specific EC regulatory networks.
source: Analysis of transcription factor (TF) gene expression and TF motifs at candidate cis-regulatory elements reveals both shared and organ-specific EC regulatory networks.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from the analysis.

claim: In the embryo, only those ECs that are adjacent to or within the central nervous system (CNS) exhibit canonical Wnt signaling.
source: In the embryo, only those ECs that are adjacent to or within the central nervous system (CNS) exhibit canonical Wnt signaling, which correlates precisely with blood-brain barrier (BBB) differentiation and Zic3 expression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding about CNS-specific Wnt signaling.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling in embryonic CNS ECs correlates precisely with blood-brain barrier (BBB) differentiation.
source: In the embryo, only those ECs that are adjacent to or within the central nervous system (CNS) exhibit canonical Wnt signaling, which correlates precisely with blood-brain barrier (BBB) differentiation and Zic3 expression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the correlation between Wnt signaling and BBB differentiation.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling in embryonic CNS ECs correlates precisely with Zic3 expression.
source: In the embryo, only those ECs that are adjacent to or within the central nervous system (CNS) exhibit canonical Wnt signaling, which correlates precisely with blood-brain barrier (BBB) differentiation and Zic3 expression.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the correlation between Wnt signaling and Zic3 expression.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs in the early postnatal brain reveals close relationships between veins and mitotic cells.
source: In the early postnatal brain, single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs reveals (1) close relationships between veins and mitotic cells and between arteries and tip cells, (2) a division of capillary ECs into vein-like and artery-like classes, and (3) new endothelial subtype markers, including new validated tip cell markers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs in the early postnatal brain reveals close relationships between arteries and tip cells.
source: In the early postnatal brain, single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs reveals (1) close relationships between veins and mitotic cells and between arteries and tip cells, (2) a division of capillary ECs into vein-like and artery-like classes, and (3) new endothelial subtype markers, including new validated tip cell markers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Capillary ECs can be divided into vein-like and artery-like classes.
source: In the early postnatal brain, single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs reveals (1) close relationships between veins and mitotic cells and between arteries and tip cells, (2) a division of capillary ECs into vein-like and artery-like classes, and (3) new endothelial subtype markers, including new validated tip cell markers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The study identified new endothelial subtype markers, including new validated tip cell markers.
source: In the early postnatal brain, single-cell RNA-seq of purified ECs reveals (1) close relationships between veins and mitotic cells and between arteries and tip cells, (2) a division of capillary ECs into vein-like and artery-like classes, and (3) new endothelial subtype markers, including new validated tip cell markers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from single-cell RNA-seq analysis.

claim: In vertebrates, the vascular and immune systems constitute the only classes of cells that come into close proximity to nearly all other cell types in the body.
source: In vertebrates, the vascular and immune systems constitute the only classes of cells that come into close proximity to nearly all other cell types in the body.
evidence: This is stated as a general biological fact in the introduction.

claim: The vascular and immune systems share the property that a small number of basic cell types are further divided into functionally and molecularly distinct subtypes.
source: These systems also share the property that a small number of basic cell types are further divided into functionally and molecularly distinct subtypes, some of which are specialized for the tissues in which they reside.
evidence: This is stated as a general biological principle in the introduction.

claim: Organ-specific molecular and cellular specialization in the vascular system is typically at the level of microvascular (capillary) endothelial cells (ECs).
source: In the vascular system, organ-specific molecular and cellular specialization is typically at the level of microvascular (capillary) endothelial cells (ECs) (Aird, 2007a; Aird, 2007b; Potente and Mäkinen, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Liver capillaries have highly permeable sinusoidal vascular endothelium.
source: The highly permeable sinusoidal vascular endothelium of the liver acts as a sieve in which ECs form a discontinuous lining to allow efficient diffusional exchange between serum and hepatocytes.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of liver capillaries.

claim: Hepatic capillaries exhibit one of the body's highest capacities for endocytosis through the expression of various classes of scavenger receptors.
source: Hepatic capillaries also exhibit one of the body's highest capacities for endocytosis through the expression of various classes of scavenger receptors (Aird, 2007b; Knolle and Wohlleber, 2016; Poisson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The vast majority of capillaries in the CNS have extremely low permeability.
source: In contrast, the vast majority of capillaries in the CNS have extremely low permeability.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of CNS capillaries.

claim: CNS ECs are characterized by reduced transcytosis, an absence of fenestrations, tight junctions between neighboring cells, and a variety of small molecule transporters and efflux pumps.
source: CNS ECs are characterized by reduced transcytosis, an absence of fenestrations, tight junctions between neighboring cells, and a variety of small molecule transporters and efflux pumps (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The properties of CNS ECs together constitute the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
source: Together, these properties constitute the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
evidence: This is stated as a definition of the BBB based on CNS EC properties.

claim: The widespread functional, morphological, and molecular heterogeneity of ECs must ultimately reflect different gene expression programs.
source: The widespread functional, morphological, and molecular heterogeneity of ECs must ultimately reflect different gene expression programs.
evidence: This is stated as a logical inference about the basis of EC heterogeneity.

claim: The BBB program involves the coordinated regulation of a large number of genes.
source: The BBB program represents a particularly interesting case, as it involves the coordinated regulation of a large number of genes (Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Early transplantation studies showed that the BBB properties of CNS ECs are induced by developing neural tissue.
source: Early transplantation studies showed that the BBB properties of CNS ECs are induced by developing neural tissue (Stewart and Wiley, 1981), implicating an instructive signal from surrounding parenchyma.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: WNT and NORRIN ligands produced by neurons and glia activate receptors on ECs.
source: More recent work has shown that WNT and NORRIN ligands produced by neurons and glia activate receptors on ECs, and the resulting canonical Wnt signal initiates and maintains the BBB state (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The canonical Wnt signal resulting from WNT and NORRIN ligands initiates and maintains the BBB state.
source: More recent work has shown that WNT and NORRIN ligands produced by neurons and glia activate receptors on ECs, and the resulting canonical Wnt signal initiates and maintains the BBB state (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The same canonical Wnt signal acts earlier in vascular development to direct CNS angiogenesis.
source: Interestingly, the same canonical Wnt signal acts earlier in vascular development to direct CNS angiogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about Wnt signaling in CNS vascular development.

claim: Most molecular studies of EC heterogeneity have focused on defining transcriptome differences between EC subtypes.
source: Most molecular studies of EC heterogeneity have focused on defining transcriptome differences between EC subtypes (Chi et al., 2003; Daneman et al., 2010; Nolan et al., 2013; Hupe et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several recent studies have investigated the enhancer landscape of ECs.
source: Several recent studies have also investigated the enhancer landscape of ECs (Ernst et al., 2011; Hogan et al., 2017; Quillien et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There have been no genome-wide analyses that integrate and compare the transcriptome, chromatin structure, and DNA methylation landscapes of ECs prior to this study.
source: However, there have been no genome-wide analyses that integrate and compare the transcriptome, chromatin structure, and DNA methylation landscapes of ECs.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Accessible chromatin and genomic regions with low levels of CG methylation mark candidate cis-regulatory elements (CREs).
source: Accessible chromatin and genomic regions with low levels of CG methylation are of particular interest as they mark candidate cis-regulatory elements (CREs) (Stadler et al., 2011; Thurman et al., 2012; Stergachis et al., 2013; Ziller et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CG hypomethylation can provide a record of a cell's developmental history.
source: Importantly, CG hypomethylation can also provide a record of a cell's developmental history, offering an opportunity to identify lineage-specific regulators (Hon et al., 2013; Mo et al., 2015; Mo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ECs were isolated from four different murine tissues - brain, liver, lung, and kidney - at postnatal day 7 (P7).
source: Toward this end, we isolated ECs from four different murine tissues - brain, liver, lung, and kidney - at postnatal day 7 (P7) and performed RNA-seq, MethylC-seq (Lister et al., 2008), and ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2013) to generate an atlas of transcript abundances, single-base resolution DNA methylation, and accessible chromatin, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: RNA-seq, MethylC-seq, and ATAC-seq were performed on isolated ECs to generate an atlas of transcript abundances, single-base resolution DNA methylation, and accessible chromatin.
source: Toward this end, we isolated ECs from four different murine tissues - brain, liver, lung, and kidney - at postnatal day 7 (P7) and performed RNA-seq, MethylC-seq (Lister et al., 2008), and ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2013) to generate an atlas of transcript abundances, single-base resolution DNA methylation, and accessible chromatin, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: At P7, the vasculature is still growing but has also presumably acquired tissue-specific properties to support organ function.
source: At P7, the vasculature is still growing but it has also, presumably, acquired tissue-specific properties to support organ function.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for choosing P7 as the developmental time point.

claim: ECs were isolated from Tie2-GFP mice, which specifically express green fluorescent protein (GFP) in ECs.
source: To isolate ECs, we harvested organs from Tie2-GFP (the Tie2 gene is also known as Tek) mice, which specifically express green fluorescent protein (GFP) in ECs (Motoike et al., 2000), enzymatically dissociated the tissues into single-cell suspensions, and then purified ECs using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the method for isolating ECs, with citation support.

claim: The approach to EC isolation was optimized and validated by Daneman et al., 2010.
source: This approach to EC isolation was optimized and validated by Daneman et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Tie2-GFP is not expressed in all ECs.
source: We note that Tie2-GFP is not expressed in all ECs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the limitations of the Tie2-GFP marker.

claim: GFP could not be detected in the capillaries of renal glomeruli by immunostaining.
source: For example, we could not detect GFP in the capillaries of renal glomeruli by immunostaining (yellow arrows in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: Each high-throughput sequencing experiment was performed on two or more independent biological replicates.
source: Each high-throughput sequencing experiment was performed on two or more independent biological replicates, and these exhibited high pairwise correlations (Figure 1A and far right panel of Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4A; Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and quality control, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Biological replicates of high-throughput sequencing experiments exhibited high pairwise correlations.
source: Each high-throughput sequencing experiment was performed on two or more independent biological replicates, and these exhibited high pairwise correlations (Figure 1A and far right panel of Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4A; Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the quality control results, with reference to figures showing the data.

claim: Slc2a1, a glucose transporter, is expressed in brain ECs.
source: Genome browser images showing CG methylation (top) and RNA expression (bottom) for two genes: Slc2a1, a glucose transporter expressed in brain ECs, and Fabp4, a fatty acid binding protein expressed in liver and kidney ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in the genome browser image.

claim: Fabp4, a fatty acid binding protein, is expressed in liver and kidney ECs.
source: Genome browser images showing CG methylation (top) and RNA expression (bottom) for two genes: Slc2a1, a glucose transporter expressed in brain ECs, and Fabp4, a fatty acid binding protein expressed in liver and kidney ECs.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in the genome browser image.

claim: Tissue-specific gene expression is associated with tissue-specific hypomethylation near the TSS.
source: For both genes, tissue-specific gene expression is associated with tissue-specific hypomethylation near the TSS.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend and shown in the genome browser image.

claim: A union set of 4117 protein-coding and non-coding EC-enriched transcripts was determined from each tissue.
source: By comparing the expression profiles of GFP-positive cells to GFP-negative cells, we determined a union set of 4117 protein-coding and non-coding EC-enriched transcripts from each tissue for further analysis (Supplementary file 2; see the RNA-seq section under Materials and methods for the three criteria applied in this comparison).
evidence: This describes the data analysis results.

claim: The list of EC-enriched transcripts contains many known EC markers, including Pecam1, Kdr, Cdh5, and Tek.
source: Importantly, this list contains many known EC markers, including Pecam1, Kdr, Cdh5, and Tek (also known as Tie2).
evidence: This validates the EC enrichment analysis by showing it captures known markers.

claim: The pan-leukocyte marker Ptprc/Cd45 is notably absent from the list of EC-enriched transcripts.
source: Notably absent from the list are the pan-leukocyte marker Ptprc/Cd45, the macrophage/microglia marker Csf1r, the vascular smooth muscle cell marker Acta2, the pericyte marker Cspg4, and various abundant parenchyma-specific markers such as Syt11 (brain), Alb (liver), Sftpc (lung), and Umod (kidney) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This validates the EC enrichment analysis by showing it excludes non-EC markers.

claim: The GFP-negative fraction of dissociated liver was unexpectedly depleted for hepatocyte-specific transcripts.
source: The GFP-negative fraction of dissociated liver was unexpectedly depleted for hepatocyte-specific transcripts suggesting that hepatocytes were lost during cell dissociation and/or flow cytometry.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about the liver sample preparation.

claim: The GFP-negative fraction of dissociated liver was enriched for transcripts associated with Kupffer cells and cholangiocytes.
source: This fraction was enriched for transcripts associated with Kupffer cells (Cd68, Cd80, and Cd86) and cholangiocytes (Epcam, Pkhd1l1, and St14; Li et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This describes the composition of the GFP-negative liver fraction, with citation support.

claim: Brain ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for transporters such as Mfsd2a, Slc2a1, and Slco1c1.
source: Brain ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for transporters such as Mfsd2a, Slc2a1, and Slco1c1 (Figure 1B, first three panels), whereas liver sinusoidal ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for scavenger receptors such as Fcgr2b, Stab2, and Clec4g (Figure 1B, first panel).
evidence: This describes tissue-specific gene expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: Liver sinusoidal ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for scavenger receptors such as Fcgr2b, Stab2, and Clec4g.
source: Brain ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for transporters such as Mfsd2a, Slc2a1, and Slco1c1 (Figure 1B, first three panels), whereas liver sinusoidal ECs specifically express mRNAs coding for scavenger receptors such as Fcgr2b, Stab2, and Clec4g (Figure 1B, first panel).
evidence: This describes tissue-specific gene expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: mRNA coding for angiotensin-converting enzyme (Ace), a known lung EC marker, was specifically enriched in lung ECs.
source: Similarly, mRNA coding for angiotensin-converting enzyme (Ace), a known lung EC marker, was specifically enriched in lung ECs (Figure 1B, second panel).
evidence: This describes tissue-specific gene expression patterns observed in the data.

claim: The differential expression analysis identified two novel lung EC markers, Scn7a and Scn3b.
source: The differential expression analysis also identified two novel lung EC markers, Scn7a and Scn3b (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplements 3B and 4B).
evidence: This describes a novel finding from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Scn7a is a sodium channel referred to as Na(x) that is responsive to extracellular levels of sodium.
source: The former is a sodium channel referred to as Na(x) that is responsive to extracellular levels of sodium and that was previously reported to be expressed in lung epithelium (Watanabe et al., 2000; Watanabe et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2015), while the latter is an auxiliary beta subunit that can modify the conductance of sodium channel alpha subunits (Cusdin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Scn7a was previously reported to be expressed in lung epithelium.
source: The former is a sodium channel referred to as Na(x) that is responsive to extracellular levels of sodium and that was previously reported to be expressed in lung epithelium (Watanabe et al., 2000; Watanabe et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2015), while the latter is an auxiliary beta subunit that can modify the conductance of sodium channel alpha subunits (Cusdin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Scn3b is an auxiliary beta subunit that can modify the conductance of sodium channel alpha subunits.
source: The former is a sodium channel referred to as Na(x) that is responsive to extracellular levels of sodium and that was previously reported to be expressed in lung epithelium (Watanabe et al., 2000; Watanabe et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2015), while the latter is an auxiliary beta subunit that can modify the conductance of sodium channel alpha subunits (Cusdin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Scn7a and Scn3b show enrichment in lung ECs on par with Ace enrichment.
source: In contrast, both Scn7a and Scn3b show a clear enrichment in lung ECs on par with Ace enrichment, implying that they function in ECs rather than in the epithelium (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern observed in the data.

claim: Expression of Scn7a and Scn3b may allow lung ECs to directly sense serum sodium concentration.
source: We speculate that expression of Scn7a and Scn3b may allow lung ECs to directly sense serum sodium concentration, perhaps to regulate Ace expression and thereby provide feedback control of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the expression data and known functions.

claim: Transcripts from 2392 genes exhibited >2 fold differential abundance between one or more pairs of EC subtypes.
source: Transcripts from 2392 genes exhibited >2 fold differential abundance between one or more pairs of EC subtypes, with 739 exhibiting >2 fold differential expression in a comparison of ECs from one tissue versus ECs from each of the other three tissues (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 2; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the results of the differential expression analysis.

claim: 739 genes exhibited >2 fold differential expression in a comparison of ECs from one tissue versus ECs from each of the other three tissues.
source: Transcripts from 2392 genes exhibited >2 fold differential abundance between one or more pairs of EC subtypes, with 739 exhibiting >2 fold differential expression in a comparison of ECs from one tissue versus ECs from each of the other three tissues (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 2; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the results of the differential expression analysis.

claim: Of the 739 ECTSGs, 685 are protein-coding and 54 are non-coding.
source: Of the 739 ECTSGs, 685 are protein-coding and 54 are non-coding.
evidence: This describes the composition of the ECTSG set.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the four sets of ECTSGs was consistent with tissue-specific specializations of each vascular bed.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (Ashburner et al., 2000; The Gene Ontology Consortium, 2017; The Gene Ontology Consortium, 2017) of the four sets of ECTSGs was consistent with tissue-specific specializations of each vascular bed.
evidence: This describes the results of the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Brain ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'neutral amino acid transport' and 'drug transmembrane transport'.
source: For example, brain ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'neutral amino acid transport' and 'drug transmembrane transport' whereas liver ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'scavenger receptor activity' and 'vesicle-mediated transport' (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the results of the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Liver ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'scavenger receptor activity' and 'vesicle-mediated transport'.
source: For example, brain ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'neutral amino acid transport' and 'drug transmembrane transport' whereas liver ECTSGs were enriched for GO terms such as 'scavenger receptor activity' and 'vesicle-mediated transport' (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the results of the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Brain ECTSGs were enriched for the GO term 'negative regulation of canonical Wnt signaling pathway'.
source: Consistent with the known role of Wnt signaling in brain endothelium development, brain ECTSGs were also enriched for the GO term 'negative regulation of canonical Wnt signaling pathway' (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes the results of the GO enrichment analysis and relates it to known biology.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the four EC transcriptomes showed that the transcriptional signatures of brain ECs and liver ECs are substantially distinct from each other and from those of lung ECs and kidney ECs.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of the four EC transcriptomes showed that the transcriptional signatures of brain ECs and liver ECs are substantially distinct from each other and from those of lung ECs and kidney ECs (Figure 1D), broadly consistent with earlier studies of embryonic and adult ECs (Daneman et al., 2010; Hupe et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the results of the PCA analysis, with citation support.

claim: Low cytosine DNA methylation (mCG) immediately downstream of transcriptional start sites (TSSs) typically correlates with increased gene expression.
source: Low cytosine DNA methylation (mCG) immediately downstream of transcriptional start sites (TSSs) typically correlates with increased gene expression (Schultz et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Differentially expressed genes are often associated with tissue-specific hypomethylation starting at the TSS and extending into the gene body.
source: In visually comparing EC methylation profiles to transcription profiles, we find that differentially expressed genes are often associated with tissue-specific hypomethylation starting at the TSS and extending into the gene body (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes an observation from comparing methylation and expression data.

claim: Plotting the mean fraction of mCG methylation in a five kilobase (kb) window downstream of the TSS for all protein-coding genes reveals an inverse relationship between methylation and gene expression among differentially expressed EC-enriched genes.
source: As a result, plotting the mean fraction of mCG methylation in a five kilobase (kb) window downstream of the TSS for all protein-coding genes reveals an inverse relationship between methylation and gene expression among differentially expressed EC-enriched genes (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the results of the methylation analysis.

claim: Differences in methylation at differentially expressed genes occur in the context of highly similar global methylation patterns.
source: However, these differences in methylation at differentially expressed genes occur in the context of highly similar global methylation patterns, as seen by correlation coefficients between different EC subtypes (0.95–0.97) that are nearly indistinguishable from the correlation coefficients between biological replicates (0.95–0.98; Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the overall similarity of methylation patterns across EC subtypes.

claim: 16,158 brain EC, 16,506 liver EC, 16,171 lung EC, and 15,979 kidney EC UMRs were identified.
source: We identified 16,158 brain EC, 16,506 liver EC, 16,171 lung EC, and 15,979 kidney EC UMRs (median length = 1738 bp; median mCG = 10%), and 72,061 brain EC, 60,212 liver EC, 57,594 lung EC, and 71,343 kidney EC LMRs (median length = 490 bp; median mCG = 15%) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the results of the UMR and LMR identification analysis.

claim: 72,061 brain EC, 60,212 liver EC, 57,594 lung EC, and 71,343 kidney EC LMRs were identified.
source: We identified 16,158 brain EC, 16,506 liver EC, 16,171 lung EC, and 15,979 kidney EC UMRs (median length = 1738 bp; median mCG = 10%), and 72,061 brain EC, 60,212 liver EC, 57,594 lung EC, and 71,343 kidney EC LMRs (median length = 490 bp; median mCG = 15%) (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the results of the UMR and LMR identification analysis.

claim: 72% of the UMRs (12,581 of 17,406) are within 2 kb of a TSS.
source: 72% of the UMRs (12,581 of 17,406) are within 2 kb of a TSS whereas only 5.7% of the LMRs (6682 of 116,273) are within 2 kb of a TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with an earlier study showing that UMRs are enriched at promoters and LMRs are enriched at distal regulatory elements (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of UMRs and LMRs, with citation support.

claim: Only 5.7% of the LMRs (6682 of 116,273) are within 2 kb of a TSS.
source: 72% of the UMRs (12,581 of 17,406) are within 2 kb of a TSS whereas only 5.7% of the LMRs (6682 of 116,273) are within 2 kb of a TSS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with an earlier study showing that UMRs are enriched at promoters and LMRs are enriched at distal regulatory elements (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of UMRs and LMRs, with citation support.

claim: 86% of UMRs (15,036 of 17,406) are shared by all four EC subtypes.
source: 86% of UMRs (15,036 of 17,406) are shared by all four EC subtypes, whereas only 25% of LMRs (29,053 of 116,273) are shared by all four EC subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of UMRs and LMRs across EC subtypes.

claim: Only 25% of LMRs (29,053 of 116,273) are shared by all four EC subtypes.
source: 86% of UMRs (15,036 of 17,406) are shared by all four EC subtypes, whereas only 25% of LMRs (29,053 of 116,273) are shared by all four EC subtypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of UMRs and LMRs across EC subtypes.

claim: 105,050 discrete differentially hypomethylated regions ('hypo-DMRs') were discovered.
source: Using a conservative statistical approach (Lister et al., 2013); see Materials and methods), we discovered 105,050 discrete differentially hypomethylated regions ('hypo-DMRs'; i.e., a % mC difference above threshold in one or more pairwise comparisons between EC tissue types; median length = 228 bp) with the largest number present in liver ECs (42,682), followed by lung ECs (32,004), brain ECs (30,471), and kidney ECs (17,027).
evidence: This describes the results of the DMR identification analysis.

claim: The largest number of hypo-DMRs are present in liver ECs (42,682), followed by lung ECs (32,004), brain ECs (30,471), and kidney ECs (17,027).
source: Using a conservative statistical approach (Lister et al., 2013); see Materials and methods), we discovered 105,050 discrete differentially hypomethylated regions ('hypo-DMRs'; i.e., a % mC difference above threshold in one or more pairwise comparisons between EC tissue types; median length = 228 bp) with the largest number present in liver ECs (42,682), followed by lung ECs (32,004), brain ECs (30,471), and kidney ECs (17,027).
evidence: This describes the distribution of hypo-DMRs across EC subtypes.

claim: A smaller number of hypo-DMRs were uniquely hypomethylated in one EC tissue type (25,612 in liver ECs, 13,862 in lung ECs, 16,540 in brain ECs, and 7132 in kidney ECs).
source: A smaller number of hypo-DMRs were uniquely hypomethylated in one EC tissue type (25,612 in liver ECs, 13,862 in lung ECs, 16,540 in brain ECs, and 7132 in kidney ECs).
evidence: This describes the number of tissue-specific hypo-DMRs.

claim: Almost all hypo-DMRs (94.5%) are found >2 kb from a TSS.
source: Almost all hypo-DMRs (94.5%) are found >2 kb from a TSS, suggesting they reflect distal regulatory elements (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of hypo-DMRs.

claim: Many closely spaced hypo-DMRs are part of larger hypomethylated regions that correlate with the current transcriptional state of a cell and with higher levels of histone modifications associated with active enhancers.
source: A previous study in neurons has shown that many closely spaced hypo-DMRs are part of larger hypomethylated regions that correlate with the current transcriptional state of a cell and with higher levels of histone modifications associated with active enhancers (Mo et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ECTS-large hypo-DMRs are enriched at differentially expressed EC-enriched genes.
source: ECTS-large hypo-DMRs are enriched at differentially expressed EC-enriched genes (q-value <10−10; Figure 2B; see Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This describes the enrichment analysis results.

claim: DNA methylation valleys (DMVs) exhibit especially high enrichment at genes coding for important regulators of embryonic development including many TFs.
source: DNA methylation valleys (DMVs; also referred to as DNA methylation canyons) are a distinct category of large hypomethylated regions that exhibit especially high enrichment at genes coding for important regulators of embryonic development including many TFs (Xie et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2014; Mo et al., 2015; Mo et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 2313 brain EC, 2695 liver EC, 2403 lung EC, and 2208 kidney EC DMVs were identified.
source: Defining DMVs as UMRs > 3 kb, we identified 2313 brain EC, 2695 liver EC, 2403 lung EC, and 2208 kidney EC DMVs (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This describes the results of the DMV identification analysis.

claim: There is very little overlap between large hypo-DMRs and DMVs.
source: We found very little overlap between large hypo-DMRs and DMVs, implying they represent distinct hypomethylated features (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the relationship between large hypo-DMRs and DMVs.

claim: 1602 DMVs are shared by all four EC subtypes.
source: These two categories of hypomethylation are further distinguished by the extent to which they are shared between EC types: 1602 DMVs are shared by all four EC subtypes and additional DMVs are shared between subsets of EC subtypes, whereas the majority of large hypo-DMRs are specific to a single EC subtype (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the overlap of DMVs across EC subtypes.

claim: The majority of large hypo-DMRs are specific to a single EC subtype.
source: These two categories of hypomethylation are further distinguished by the extent to which they are shared between EC types: 1602 DMVs are shared by all four EC subtypes and additional DMVs are shared between subsets of EC subtypes, whereas the majority of large hypo-DMRs are specific to a single EC subtype (Figure 2C).
evidence: This describes the tissue-specificity of large hypo-DMRs.

claim: EC DMVs are highly enriched for genes encoding TFs.
source: Consistent with previous studies in other tissues (Xie et al., 2013; Jeong et al., 2014; Mo et al., 2015; Mo et al., 2016), EC DMVs are highly enriched for genes encoding TFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This describes the gene ontology enrichment results for DMVs, with citation support.

claim: Previously identified DMVs in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) remain hypomethylated after cellular differentiation.
source: Previously identified DMVs in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) remain hypomethylated after cellular differentiation, with only a small subset demonstrating DNA methylation variations across cell types (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Large regions of hypomethylation (DMVs) are maintained by Polycomb complexes that deposit repressive H3K27me3 histone modifications.
source: These large regions of hypomethylation are maintained by Polycomb complexes that deposit repressive H3K27me3 histone modifications and are thought to support developmental plasticity, as DNA methylation may reflect a more stable repressive mechanism (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DMVs are thought to support developmental plasticity.
source: These large regions of hypomethylation are maintained by Polycomb complexes that deposit repressive H3K27me3 histone modifications and are thought to support developmental plasticity, as DNA methylation may reflect a more stable repressive mechanism (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In all four subtypes of ECs, DMVs overlap Etv2, Foxc2, Tal1, Lmo2, Id3, and Fli1, genes coding for TFs that are important for establishing the EC lineage.
source: In all four subtypes of ECs, DMVs overlap Etv2, Foxc2, Tal1, Lmo2, Id3, and Fli1, genes coding for TFs that are important for establishing the EC lineage (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of DMVs with specific TF genes.

claim: DMVs are also present at Sox7, Hey1, and Nr2f2, TFs important for venous or arterial differentiation.
source: DMVs are also present at Sox7, Hey1, and Nr2f2, TFs important for venous or arterial differentiation.
evidence: This describes the overlap of DMVs with specific TF genes.

claim: The early embryonic TF gene Pou5f1/Oct4 lacks a DMV.
source: An exception to this pattern is seen with the early embryonic TF gene Pou5f1/Oct4, which lacks a DMV, consistent with a previous report that this locus exhibits increased DNA methylation upon cell differentiation (Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the absence of a DMV at a specific gene, with citation support.

claim: No EC DMVs overlap Gata1 and Spi1, which are important for establishing the erythroid and myeloid/lymphoid lineages, respectively.
source: No EC DMVs overlap Gata1 and Spi1, which are important for establishing the erythroid and myeloid/lymphoid lineages, respectively.
evidence: This describes the absence of DMVs at specific genes.

claim: DMVs occur at TFs that determine very early progenitor cell lineage commitments.
source: Given that ECs and hematopoietic cells share the same developmental lineage, these observations suggest that DMVs occur at TFs that determine very early progenitor cell lineage commitments.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the DMV overlap patterns.

claim: EC DMVs overlap some genes coding for lineage-determining TFs in completely unrelated cell types, including oligodendrocytes (Olig1 and Olig2) and Muller glia (Lhx2).
source: Curiously, EC DMVs overlap some genes coding for lineage-determining TFs in completely unrelated cell types, including oligodendrocytes (Olig1 and Olig2) and Muller glia (Lhx2) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of DMVs with specific TF genes.

claim: At genes coding for TFs that are differentially expressed among EC subtypes, DMVs show EC subtype-specific differences in boundary locations and degree of methylation.
source: At genes coding for TFs that are differentially expressed among EC subtypes, DMVs show EC subtype-specific differences in boundary locations and degree of methylation, with a broad trend of increased methylation 5' of the TSS in the EC subtype(s) that express the TF gene as seen for Foxf1, Foxf2, and Zic3 in brain; Tbx3 in brain, lung, and kidney; Tbx2, Gata6, Meis1, and Meis2 in liver, lung, and kidney; Gata4 in liver; and Irx3 in kidney (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This describes the relationship between DMV methylation patterns and TF gene expression.

claim: Cell-type-specific expression of important TF regulators of lineage identity results in nearby hypermethylation.
source: This observation is consistent with a proposed model in which cell-type-specific expression of important TF regulators of lineage identity results in nearby hypermethylation (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: FOXF1, a lung EC-enriched TF, is implicated in pulmonary vascular development.
source: We note that FOXF1, a lung EC-enriched TF implicated in pulmonary vascular development (Kalinichenko et al., 2001; Cai et al., 2016; Dharmadhikari et al., 2016), represents an exception to this methylation pattern, due to demethylation at the adjacent lung EC-expressed lncRNA gene, Fendrr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HOX genes do not exhibit the classic relationship between methylation and gene expression.
source: HOX genes do not exhibit the classic relationship between methylation and gene expression (Laurent et al., 2010; Bock et al., 2012; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Among the four EC subtypes, HOX cluster DNA methylation is lowest in brain ECs, intermediate in liver and lung ECs, and highest in kidney ECs.
source: Among the four EC subtypes, HOX cluster DNA methylation is lowest in brain ECs, intermediate in liver and lung ECs, and highest in kidney ECs (Figure 3A and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methylation patterns observed in the HOX clusters.

claim: The pattern of HOX cluster methylation correlates with the anterior/posterior position of the brain, liver, lung, and kidney along the body axis.
source: This pattern of methylation correlates with the anterior/posterior position of the brain, liver, lung, and kidney – as well as with their embryonic primordia - along the body axis: the brain is most anterior, the lungs and liver are intermediate (and are derived from the primitive foregut), and the kidneys are the most posterior (and are derived from the ureteric bud and surrounding mesenchyme).
evidence: This describes the correlation between methylation patterns and anatomical position.

claim: For all four HOX clusters, the ATAC-seq patterns are similar for liver, lung, and kidney ECs, but the peak intensities are greatly reduced in brain ECs.
source: For all four HOX clusters, the ATAC-seq patterns are similar for liver, lung, and kidney ECs, but the peak intensities are greatly reduced in brain ECs (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the ATAC-seq patterns observed in the HOX clusters.

claim: In the HOX clusters, there is a roughly co-linear relationship between each gene's position along the chromosome and the anterior/posterior territory along the body axis where that HOX gene is expressed.
source: In the HOX clusters, there is a roughly co-linear relationship between each gene's position along the chromosome and the anterior/posterior territory along the body axis where that HOX gene is expressed: genes that are named with low numbers (e.g. Hoxa1) are expressed more anteriorly and genes that are named with high numbers (e.g. Hoxa13) are expressed more posteriorly (Lewis, 1978; reviewed in Papageorgiou, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Patterns of HOX gene expression correlate with the anterior/posterior position of each organ and its corresponding EC subtype.
source: Based on the EC subtype-specific RNA-seq data, we found that patterns of HOX gene expression correlate with the anterior/posterior position of each organ and its corresponding EC subtype (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This describes the correlation between HOX gene expression and anatomical position.

claim: In the HOX-A cluster, brain ECs express none of the Hoxa genes.
source: In the HOX-A cluster, brain ECs express none of the Hoxa genes; liver ECs express Hoxa2–Hoxa5; lung ECs express Hoxa2–Hoxa5 and Hoxa7; and kidney ECs express Hoxa5 and Hoxa7-Hoxa10, with lower levels of expression in Hoxa2-Hoxa4. (Figure 3B and D).
evidence: This describes the HOX gene expression patterns in different EC subtypes.

claim: There does not appear to be a strong relationship between HOX gene expression and gene body methylation.
source: Interestingly, there does not appear to be a strong relationship between gene expression and gene body methylation (compare top and bottom heatmaps in Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes the lack of correlation between HOX gene expression and gene body methylation.

claim: Expression of a HOX gene correlates with increased methylation in the neighborhood of the gene body.
source: Rather, like other developmentally important TFs, the trend is that expression of a HOX gene correlates with increased methylation in the neighborhood of the gene body.
evidence: This describes the relationship between HOX gene expression and nearby methylation.

claim: For each of the four organs, the patterns of EC and parenchymal cell expression of Hoxa genes are closely matched.
source: For each of the four organs, the patterns of EC and parenchymal cell expression of Hoxa genes are closely matched (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the similarity of HOX gene expression between ECs and parenchymal cells.

claim: A microarray transcriptome meta-analysis showed a correlation between patterns of HOX gene expression and the tissue-of-origin for a collection of human EC lines.
source: These data confirm and extend two earlier studies: (1) a microarray transcriptome meta-analysis showing a correlation between patterns of HOX gene expression and the tissue-of-origin for a collection of human EC lines (Toshner et al., 2014) and (2) a transgenic mouse study showing that Hoxa3 and Hoxc11 reporter expression in murine vasculature roughly corresponds to the positional identity specified by the HOX code (Pruett et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A transgenic mouse study showed that Hoxa3 and Hoxc11 reporter expression in murine vasculature roughly corresponds to the positional identity specified by the HOX code.
source: These data confirm and extend two earlier studies: (1) a microarray transcriptome meta-analysis showing a correlation between patterns of HOX gene expression and the tissue-of-origin for a collection of human EC lines (Toshner et al., 2014) and (2) a transgenic mouse study showing that Hoxa3 and Hoxc11 reporter expression in murine vasculature roughly corresponds to the positional identity specified by the HOX code (Pruett et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The patterns of HOX gene expression and DNA methylation suggest that ECs in different organs 'know' their anterior-posterior position within the body.
source: Taken together, the patterns of HOX gene expression and DNA methylation suggest that ECs in different organs 'know' their anterior-posterior position within the body.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the HOX gene expression and methylation data.

claim: A total of 51,740 discrete regions of accessible chromatin (i.e. ATAC-seq peaks) were identified among the four EC subtypes using the full range of ATAC-seq fragment lengths.
source: In our initial analysis, we used the full range of ATAC-seq fragment lengths and identified a total of 51,740 discrete regions of accessible chromatin (i.e. ATAC-seq peaks; median length 656 bp) among the four EC subtypes (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This describes the results of the ATAC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: Across replicates, the percent of mapped reads found in called peaks ranged between 16 and 34%.
source: Across replicates, the percent of mapped reads found in called peaks ranged between 16 and 34% (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the quality control metrics for the ATAC-seq data.

claim: With the sequencing depth used, the ATAC-seq data is approaching an asymptote.
source: Calling peaks on subsamples of total mapped reads for each ATAC-seq replicate indicates that, with this sequencing depth, the data is approaching an asymptote (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the saturation analysis for the ATAC-seq data.

claim: Using <100 bp fragments, a total of 39,987 ATAC-seq peaks were identified among the four EC subtypes.
source: Using <100 bp fragments, we identified a total of 39,987 ATAC-seq peaks (median length 508 bp) among the four EC subtypes (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This describes the results of the ATAC-seq peak calling analysis using short fragments.

claim: Of the ATAC-seq peaks identified, 35% are shared across all four EC subtypes, but only 1–16% are EC subtype-specific.
source: Of the 31,358 brain EC, 18,926 liver EC, 24,970 lung EC, and 21,694 kidney EC ATAC-seq peaks, 35% are shared across all four EC subtypes, but only 1–16% are EC subtype-specific (6381 brain, 632 liver, 755 lung, and 397 kidney EC-tissue-specific ATAC-seq peaks, referred to hereafter as 'ECTSAPs') (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes the overlap of ATAC-seq peaks across EC subtypes.

claim: Multiple ECTSAPs are observed near ECTSGs.
source: We observed multiple ECTSAPs near ECTSGs, as illustrated in Figure 4A using the full range of ATAC-seq fragment lengths.
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between ECTSAPs and ECTSGs.

claim: ECTS-hypo-DMRs generally co-localize with ECTSAPs.
source: As indicated by the translucent orange bars in Figure 4A, ECTS-hypo-DMRs generally co-localize with ECTSAPs.
evidence: This describes the co-localization of ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs.

claim: ECTSAPs for each tissue type are enriched near differentially expressed EC-enriched genes for that tissue.
source: In scatter plots of normalized ATAC-seq read densities, ECTSAPs for each tissue type are enriched near differentially expressed EC-enriched genes for that tissue (Figure 4B), and broad differences are apparent between EC subtypes (r = 0.75–0.92), whereas biological replicates of the same subtype are highly similar (r = 0.93–0.97, Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the enrichment of ECTSAPs near differentially expressed genes.

claim: A larger proportion of ECTSAPs and ECTS-hypo-DMRs are within 100 kb of ECTSGs that are expressed in the corresponding EC subtype relative to ECTSGs expressed in the other EC subtypes.
source: Additionally, a larger proportion of ECTSAPs and ECTS-hypo-DMRs are within 100 kb of ECTSGs that are expressed in the corresponding EC subtype relative to ECTSGs expressed in the other EC subtypes, a difference that is highly significant statistically (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This describes the enrichment of ECTSAPs and ECTS-hypo-DMRs near ECTSGs.

claim: Of the 39,987 total ATAC-seq peaks among all four EC subtypes, 64% are >2 kb from a TSS (i.e. are promoter-distal).
source: Of the 39,987 total ATAC-seq peaks among all four EC subtypes, 64% are >2 kb from a TSS (i.e. are promoter-distal).
evidence: This describes the genomic distribution of ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: A majority of promoter-proximal (<2 kb from a TSS) ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (10,336 of 14,474; 71%).
source: Similar to the distributions described above for UMRs and LMRs, a majority of promoter-proximal (<2 kb from a TSS) ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (10,336 of 14,474; 71%), whereas only a small minority of promoter-distal ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (3476 of 25,517; 14%) (Figure 4C, upper two panels; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of promoter-proximal ATAC-seq peaks across EC subtypes.

claim: Only a small minority of promoter-distal ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (3476 of 25,517; 14%).
source: Similar to the distributions described above for UMRs and LMRs, a majority of promoter-proximal (<2 kb from a TSS) ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (10,336 of 14,474; 71%), whereas only a small minority of promoter-distal ATAC-seq peaks are shared by all EC subtypes (3476 of 25,517; 14%) (Figure 4C, upper two panels; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This describes the overlap of promoter-distal ATAC-seq peaks across EC subtypes.

claim: The ATAC-seq comparisons reveal a greater degree of similarity in chromatin accessibility among ECs derived from the three peripheral tissue (liver, lung, and kidney) relative to brain ECs.
source: The ATAC-seq comparisons also reveal a greater degree of similarity in chromatin accessibility among ECs derived from the three peripheral tissue (liver, lung, and kidney) relative to brain ECs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This describes the similarity of chromatin accessibility across EC subtypes.

claim: The heterogeneity in gene expression that gives rise to tissue-specific EC differentiation may largely reflect differences in distal rather than proximal CREs.
source: Taken together, these comparisons suggest that the heterogeneity in gene expression that gives rise to tissue-specific EC differentiation may largely reflect differences in distal rather than proximal CREs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the ATAC-seq and methylation data.

claim: In all four EC subtypes, >80% of ATAC-seq peaks overlap with UMRs or LMRs.
source: In all four EC subtypes, >80% of ATAC-seq peaks overlap with UMRs or LMRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), in agreement with previous findings in neurons and photoreceptors (Mo et al., 2015; Mo et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the overlap between ATAC-seq peaks and hypomethylated regions, with citation support.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks from all four EC subtypes exhibit similarly reduced levels of DNA methylation compared to random size-matched genomic regions.
source: ATAC-seq peaks from all four EC subtypes exhibit similarly reduced levels of DNA methylation compared to random size-matched genomic regions.
evidence: This describes the relationship between chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.

claim: ECTSAPs exhibit levels of DNA methylation that are preferentially reduced in their respective EC DNA methylomes.
source: Moreover, ECTSAPs exhibit levels of DNA methylation that are preferentially reduced in their respective EC DNA methylomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This describes the tissue-specific relationship between chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.

claim: There were preferential increases in the EC subtype-specific ATAC-seq signal in the respective ECTS-hypo-DMRs.
source: Reciprocally, there were preferential increases in the EC subtype-specific ATAC-seq signal in the respective ECTS-hypo-DMRs (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This describes the tissue-specific relationship between chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation.

claim: There are many more LMRs than ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Interestingly, there are many more LMRs than ATAC-seq peaks, and therefore only a minority of LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks:<10% of liver EC and kidney EC LMRs and <20% of brain and lung EC LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This describes the numerical difference between LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Only a minority of LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Interestingly, there are many more LMRs than ATAC-seq peaks, and therefore only a minority of LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks:<10% of liver EC and kidney EC LMRs and <20% of brain and lung EC LMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This describes the overlap between LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: >75% of UMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks in all four EC subtypes.
source: In contrast, >75% of UMRs overlap with ATAC-seq peaks in all four EC subtypes.
evidence: This describes the overlap between UMRs and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: <5% of liver EC, lung EC, and kidney EC hypo-DMRs overlap with their respective ATAC-seq peaks.
source: In comparing ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs, <5% of liver EC, lung EC, and kidney EC hypo-DMRs overlap with their respective ATAC-seq peaks, whereas 13% of brain EC hypo-DMRs overlap with brain ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: This describes the overlap between ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs.

claim: 13% of brain EC hypo-DMRs overlap with brain ATAC-seq peaks.
source: In comparing ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs, <5% of liver EC, lung EC, and kidney EC hypo-DMRs overlap with their respective ATAC-seq peaks, whereas 13% of brain EC hypo-DMRs overlap with brain ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: This describes the overlap between ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs.

claim: Many distal enhancer regions may not exhibit a sufficient degree of chromatin accessibility to permit insertion by two transposon complexes, the requisite event for detection of DNA accessibility by ATAC-seq.
source: As two explanations for this numerical difference, we suggest either (1) that many distal enhancer regions may not exhibit a sufficient degree of chromatin accessibility to permit insertion by two transposon complexes, the requisite event for detection of DNA accessibility by ATAC-seq, or (2) that distal enhancer regions may have greater variance in their occupancy across the population of cells, resulting in a general decrease in average accessibility.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the discrepancy between hypomethylated regions and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: Distal enhancer regions may have greater variance in their occupancy across the population of cells, resulting in a general decrease in average accessibility.
source: As two explanations for this numerical difference, we suggest either (1) that many distal enhancer regions may not exhibit a sufficient degree of chromatin accessibility to permit insertion by two transposon complexes, the requisite event for detection of DNA accessibility by ATAC-seq, or (2) that distal enhancer regions may have greater variance in their occupancy across the population of cells, resulting in a general decrease in average accessibility.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for the discrepancy between hypomethylated regions and ATAC-seq peaks.

claim: If LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks mark CREs, then they should be enriched for the DNA binding motifs of the TFs that control the distinct transcriptional, chromatin, and DNA methylation landscapes observed in ECs from different tissues.
source: If LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks mark CREs, then they should be enriched for the DNA binding motifs of the TFs that control the distinct transcriptional, chromatin, and DNA methylation landscapes observed in ECs from different tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on models of transcriptional regulation.

claim: Current models of transcriptional regulation posit that TFs act in a combinatorial fashion, co-localizing at CREs to give rise to cell-type-specific transcription.
source: Current models of transcriptional regulation posit that TFs act in a combinatorial fashion, co-localizing at CREs to give rise to cell-type-specific transcription (Heinz and Glass, 2011; Heinz et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CREs in different EC subtypes should share motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression common to all ECs.
source: These models predict that CREs in different EC subtypes should (1) share motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression common to all ECs, and (2) exhibit subtype-specific motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression distinctive to each EC subtype.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on models of transcriptional regulation.

claim: CREs in different EC subtypes should exhibit subtype-specific motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression distinctive to each EC subtype.
source: These models predict that CREs in different EC subtypes should (1) share motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression common to all ECs, and (2) exhibit subtype-specific motifs corresponding to TFs that orchestrate patterns of gene expression distinctive to each EC subtype.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on models of transcriptional regulation.

claim: Analyzing the common subset of EC-only LMRs and ATAC-seq peaks using HOMER revealed a highly significant enrichment for a sequence that resembles the binding motif of class 1 members of the ETS family of TFs.
source: Analyzing this common subset using HOMER revealed a highly significant (LMRs: p-value=10−1691; ATAC-seq peaks: p-value=10−148) enrichment over random GC-matched genomic regions for a sequence that resembles the binding motif of class 1 members of the ETS family of TFs, which includes ERG, FLI1, ETV2, and ETS1 (Wei et al., 2010; Hollenhorst et al., 2011); Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis, with citation support.

claim: The finding of a common enriched class 1 ETS family motif is not unexpected given the large body of data supporting a role for class 1 ETS TFs in EC development and function.
source: The finding of a common enriched class 1 ETS family motif is not unexpected given the large body of data supporting a role for class 1 ETS TFs in EC development and function (McLaughlin et al., 2001; Pham et al., 2007; Meadows et al., 2011; Oh et al., 2015; Sumanas and Choi, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: K-mers matching the SOX and GATA binding motifs were detected in shared EC-only LMRs.
source: We also detected k-mers matching the SOX (p-value=10−101) and GATA (p-value=10−94) binding motifs in shared EC-only LMRs and - unexpectedly - a k-mer matching the telomere sequence TTAGGG (p-value=10−123) in shared EC-only ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: A k-mer matching the telomere sequence TTAGGG was unexpectedly detected in shared EC-only ATAC-seq peaks.
source: We also detected k-mers matching the SOX (p-value=10−101) and GATA (p-value=10−94) binding motifs in shared EC-only LMRs and - unexpectedly - a k-mer matching the telomere sequence TTAGGG (p-value=10−123) in shared EC-only ATAC-seq peaks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: The class 1 ETS motif was found in both ECTSAPs and ECTS-hypo-DMRs.
source: To address the second prediction, we used HOMER to search for TF motifs in sequences present in the four sets of ECTSAPs and the four sets of ECTS-hypo-DMRs. In addition to the EC subtype-specific enriched motifs described in the paragraphs below, this analysis revealed the class 1 ETS motif in both ECTSAPs (p-value=10−45–10−718) and ECTS-hypo-DMRs (p-value=10−30–10−1169) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: ETS family TFs not only act in shared CREs to determine and maintain common aspects of the EC phenotype, but they also cooperate with EC subtype-specific TFs in EC subtype-specific CREs.
source: This observation suggests that ETS family TFs not only act in shared CREs to determine and maintain common aspects of the EC phenotype, but they also cooperate with EC subtype-specific TFs in EC subtype-specific CREs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the motif enrichment data.

claim: All four subtypes of ECs express members of the ETS family of TFs, including ERG, FLI1, and ETS1.
source: As determined from the EC RNA-seq datasets, all four subtypes of ECs express members of the ETS family of TFs, including ERG, FLI1, and ETS1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of ETS family TFs in ECs.

claim: HOMER identified several EC subtype-specific enriched motifs.
source: Significantly, HOMER identified several EC subtype-specific enriched motifs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: In brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs, enriched k-mers closely match the motifs of the Forkhead box (FOX), TCF/LEF, and ZIC TF families.
source: In brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs, we identified enriched k-mers that closely match the motifs of the Forkhead box (FOX), TCF/LEF, and ZIC TF families (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis for brain ECs.

claim: Transcripts corresponding to three Fox family members (Foxq1, Foxc1, and Foxf2), two Tcf/Lef family members (Tcf7 and Lef1), and the Zic family member Zic3 were highly enriched in brain ECs.
source: Transcripts corresponding to three Fox family members (Foxq1, Foxc1, and Foxf2), two Tcf/Lef family members (Tcf7 and Lef1), and the Zic family member Zic3 were highly enriched in brain ECs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of specific TFs in brain ECs.

claim: LEF/TCF family members are the effectors of canonical Wnt signaling in the nucleus.
source: LEF/TCF family members are the effectors of canonical Wnt signaling in the nucleus (Cadigan and Waterman, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The specific enrichment of LEF/TCF motifs in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs is consistent with previous evidence that canonical Wnt signaling in ECs plays a central role in CNS angiogenesis and BBB development and maintenance.
source: The specific enrichment of LEF/TCF motifs in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs and ECTSAPs is consistent with previous evidence that canonical Wnt signaling in ECs plays a central role in CNS angiogenesis and BBB development and maintenance, but that it has little or no role in vascular development outside of the CNS (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The brain EC-specific enrichment of ZIC motifs is consistent with previous work showing that the accumulation of ZIC3 in the developing retinal vasculature depends on NORRIN/FRIZZLED4 (i.e. canonical Wnt) signaling.
source: The brain EC-specific enrichment of ZIC motifs is consistent with previous work showing that the accumulation of ZIC3 in the developing retinal vasculature depends on NORRIN/FRIZZLED4 (i.e. canonical Wnt) signaling (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Analysis of candidate CREs near the Zic3 gene in all four EC subtypes revealed the presence of a brain ECTSAP ~50 kb downstream of the gene that contains ETS and TCF/LEF binding sites.
source: Analysis of candidate CREs near the Zic3 gene in all four EC subtypes revealed the presence of a brain ECTSAP ~50 kb downstream of the gene that contains ETS and TCF/LEF binding sites, suggestive of a nearby Wnt-responsive enhancer element (translucent orange bar in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This describes the identification of a candidate Wnt-responsive enhancer near Zic3.

claim: In liver ECTS-hypo-DMRs, enriched k-mers closely match the motifs recognized by members of the GATA and MAF TF families.
source: In liver ECTS-hypo-DMRs, we identified enriched k-mers that closely match the motifs recognized by members of the GATA and MAF TF families (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis for liver ECs.

claim: RNA-seq across the four EC populations showed that Gata4 and Maf have the greatest enrichment among members of their respective families in liver ECs.
source: RNA-seq across the four EC populations showed that Gata4 and Maf have the greatest enrichment among members of their respective families in liver ECs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of specific TFs in liver ECs.

claim: A recent study found that GATA4 controls liver EC development and function.
source: Consistent with these observations, a recent study found that GATA4 controls liver EC development and function (Géraud et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In liver ECTS-hypo-DMRs, enrichment was detected for a k-mer that corresponds to the NR2F2/COUP-TFII motif.
source: In liver ECTS-hypo-DMRs, we also detected enrichment for a k-mer that corresponds to the NR2F2/COUP-TFII motif (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis for liver ECs.

claim: NR2F2/COUP-TFII is essential for establishing venous EC identity.
source: As NR2F2/COUP-TFII is essential for establishing venous EC identity (You et al., 2005), enrichment of this motif could reflect enrichment of venous ECs due to inclusion of the portal vein and its tributaries or a bona fide role for NR2F2 in liver sinusoid development.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Nr2f2 transcripts are enriched in liver ECs.
source: Like Gata4 and Maf, Nr2f2 transcripts are enriched in liver ECs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of Nr2f2 in liver ECs.

claim: In lung ECTS-hypo-DMRs, enriched k-mers closely match the motifs of the FOX, GATA, and homeobox TF families.
source: In lung ECTS-hypo-DMRs, we identified enriched k-mers that closely match the motifs of the FOX, GATA, and homeobox TF families (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis for lung ECs.

claim: Foxp1, Foxm1, Foxf1, Gata2, Gata3, Gata6, and Hoxa5 transcripts are enriched in lung ECs.
source: Foxp1, Foxm1, Foxf1, Gata2, Gata3, Gata6, and Hoxa5 transcripts are enriched in lung ECs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of specific TFs in lung ECs.

claim: In kidney ECTS-hypo-DMRs, enriched k-mers closely match the homeobox motif.
source: In kidney ECTS-hypo-DMRs, we identified enriched k-mers that closely match the homeobox motif (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis for kidney ECs.

claim: RNA-seq shows strong kidney-specific enrichment for homeobox transcripts Irx3, Hoxa7, Pbx1, and Meis2.
source: RNA-seq shows strong kidney-specific enrichment for homeobox transcripts Irx3, Hoxa7, Pbx1, and Meis2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes the expression of specific TFs in kidney ECs.

claim: A motif corresponding to anterior HOX proteins was enriched in lung and kidney.
source: A motif corresponding to anterior HOX proteins (e.g. HOXA2; Figure 5B) was enriched in lung and kidney whereas a motif corresponding to posterior HOX proteins (e.g. HOXC9; Figure 5B) showed enrichment primarily in kidney, consistent with the Hox gene expression patterns described above (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: A motif corresponding to posterior HOX proteins showed enrichment primarily in kidney.
source: A motif corresponding to anterior HOX proteins (e.g. HOXA2; Figure 5B) was enriched in lung and kidney whereas a motif corresponding to posterior HOX proteins (e.g. HOXC9; Figure 5B) showed enrichment primarily in kidney, consistent with the Hox gene expression patterns described above (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the results of the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: ECTS-hypo-DMRs found within 100 kb of ECTSGs exhibit statistically significant enrichment for most of the motifs identified in the motif enrichment analysis.
source: Consistent with this expectation, ECTS-hypo-DMRs found within 100 kb of ECTSGs exhibit statistically significant enrichment for most of the motifs in Figure 5A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the enrichment of TF motifs near ECTSGs.

claim: ECTSAPs within 100 kb of ECTSGs were also significantly enriched for several of the motifs identified in the motif enrichment analysis.
source: ECTSAPs within 100 kb of ECTSGs were also significantly enriched for several of these motifs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the enrichment of TF motifs near ECTSGs.

claim: A spike in ZIC3 motif frequency was observed precisely 2 bp from the end of and in the same orientation as the ERG motif only in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs.
source: Here, we observed a spike in ZIC3 motif frequency precisely 2 bp from the end of and in the same orientation as the ERG motif only in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs (red arrow in Figure 5D lower right panel).
evidence: This describes the spatial relationship between ERG and ZIC3 motifs.

claim: The proximity, precise spacing, and orientation of the ERG and ZIC3 motifs in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs suggests that these two transcription factors form a ternary complex by binding to this larger DNA element.
source: The proximity, precise spacing, and orientation of the ERG and ZIC3 motifs in brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs suggests that these two transcription factors form a ternary complex by binding to this larger DNA element.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the motif spacing data.

claim: HOMER analysis on brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs with longer motifs revealed a consensus motif referred to as the paired ETS:ZIC motif.
source: To determine a consensus for this element, we repeated the HOMER analysis on brain ECTS-hypo-DMRs with longer motifs. This analysis revealed a consensus motif that we will refer to as the paired ETS:ZIC motif (Figure 5E; Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This describes the identification of the paired ETS:ZIC motif.

claim: Identically spaced ETS and ZIC motifs lead to robust enhancer activity in the ascidian Ciona.
source: Strikingly, identically spaced ETS and ZIC motifs lead to robust enhancer activity in the ascidian Ciona, implying an ancient and conserved role for the cooperation of ETS factors and ZIC factors in transcriptional regulation (Farley et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Genome-wide, there are only 1944 instances of the paired ETS:ZIC motif.
source: Genome-wide, there are only 1944 instances of the paired ETS:ZIC motif, and this paired motif is significantly enriched in candidate brain EC CREs (both hypo-DMRs and ATAC-seq peaks) relative to random GC-matched genomic regions (DMR p-value=10−45; ATAC peak p-value=10−17) and to peripheral EC CREs (DMR p-value=10−74; ATAC peak p-value=10−7; Figure 5F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This describes the enrichment of the paired ETS:ZIC motif in brain EC CREs.

claim: 81% of the brain EC CREs that contain one or more paired ETS:ZIC motifs overlap the long terminal repeats (LTRs) of the mouse-specific endogenous retrovirus (ERV) family RLTR45/ERVB4_2.
source: Interestingly, 81% of the brain EC CREs that contain one or more paired ETS:ZIC motifs overlap the long terminal repeats (LTRs) of the mouse-specific endogenous retrovirus (ERV) family RLTR45/ERVB4_2.
evidence: This describes the overlap of the paired ETS:ZIC motif with a specific ERV family.

claim: Transposable elements, especially LTR retrotransposons, provide a rich genomic substrate for the evolution of non-coding regulatory elements.
source: Transposable elements, especially LTR retrotransposons, provide a rich genomic substrate for the evolution of non-coding regulatory elements (Emera and Wagner, 2012; Chuong et al., 2013; Chuong et al., 2016); reviewed in Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RLTR45/ERVB4_2 may represent an example of a transposable element family that is being co-opted into host gene regulatory networks that utilize ETS and ZIC factors.
source: We speculate that RLTR45/ERVB4_2 may represent an example of a transposable element family that is being co-opted into host gene regulatory networks that utilize ETS and ZIC factors.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the overlap data.

claim: It is not known whether CNS EC-specific effects of canonical Wnt signaling reflect a spatial restriction on Wnt signaling or whether canonical Wnt signaling occurs throughout the vasculature but has different downstream consequences in CNS and non-CNS tissues.
source: At present, it is not known whether CNS EC-specific effects of canonical Wnt signaling reflect a spatial restriction on Wnt signaling - perhaps reflecting the spatial distribution of the relevant ligands - or whether canonical Wnt signaling occurs throughout the vasculature but has different downstream consequences in CNS and non-CNS tissues.
evidence: This is stated as an open question about Wnt signaling in ECs.

claim: Canonical Wnt signaling was visualized at cellular resolution in CNS and non-CNS vasculature using an EC-specific Cre recombinase (Tie2-Cre) and a Cre-dependent Wnt reporter (R26-Tcf/Lef-LSL-H2B-GFP-6xMYC).
source: To address this question, we visualized canonical Wnt signaling at cellular resolution in CNS and non-CNS vasculature using an EC-specific Cre recombinase (Tie2-Cre) and a Cre-dependent Wnt reporter (R26-Tcf/Lef-LSL-H2B-GFP-6xMYC).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to visualize Wnt signaling.

claim: At E13.5, BBB development is already underway, as judged by the accumulation of the glucose transporter GLUT1/SLC2A1, a BBB marker, specifically in CNS and perineural ECs.
source: At this stage, BBB development is already underway, as judged by the accumulation of the glucose transporter GLUT1/SLC2A1, a BBB marker, specifically in CNS and perineural ECs (Figure 6B and B').
evidence: This describes the developmental stage of BBB formation at E13.5.

claim: At E13.5, ZIC3 accumulation in the vasculature is limited to CNS and perineural ECs.
source: At E13.5, ZIC3 accumulation in the vasculature is also limited to CNS and perineural ECs (Figure 6C and C'; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), a distribution that closely matches that of GLUT1/SLC2A1.
