evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of ZIC3 expression at E13.5.

claim: Vascular accumulation of LEF1, which is both a mediator and a marker of canonical Wnt signaling, is limited to CNS and perineural ECs.
source: Similarly, vascular accumulation of LEF1, which is both a mediator and a marker of canonical Wnt signaling, is limited to CNS and perineural ECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and A').
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of LEF1 expression.

claim: Visualizing the accumulation of the Wnt reporter, H2B-GFP-6xMYC, with anti-MYC immunostaining shows a neural and perineural distribution, closely matching that of SLC2A1, ZIC3, and LEF1.
source: Visualizing the accumulation of the Wnt reporter, H2B-GFP-6xMYC, with anti-MYC immunostaining shows a neural and perineural distribution, closely matching that of SLC2A1, ZIC3, and LEF1 (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of Wnt reporter activity.

claim: Cells positive for the Wnt reporter occur outside of the CNS, yet their rounded morphology and lack of association with blood vessels suggests that these cells are macrophages or other immune cells.
source: We note that cells positive for the Wnt reporter occur outside of the CNS, yet their rounded morphology and lack of association with blood vessels suggests that these cells are macrophages or other immune cells, consistent with the specificity of Tie2-Cre.
evidence: This is stated as an observation and inference about non-vascular Wnt reporter-positive cells.

claim: At P7, H2B-GFP-6xMYC accumulates in CNS ECs, as well as ECs in the renal medulla.
source: At P7, H2B-GFP-6xMYC accumulates in CNS ECs, as well as ECs in the renal medulla (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E), and ZIC3 and SLC2A1 are restricted to the CNS vasculature (data not shown).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of Wnt reporter activity at P7.

claim: At P7, ZIC3 and SLC2A1 are restricted to the CNS vasculature.
source: At P7, H2B-GFP-6xMYC accumulates in CNS ECs, as well as ECs in the renal medulla (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–E), and ZIC3 and SLC2A1 are restricted to the CNS vasculature (data not shown).
evidence: This describes the spatial distribution of ZIC3 and SLC2A1 expression at P7.

claim: The protein distributions of Wnt signaling components are consistent with the CNS EC-specific expression of Lef1 and Zic3 found by RNA-seq.
source: These protein distributions are consistent with the CNS EC-specific expression of Lef1 and Zic3 found by RNA-seq (Figure 5C) and the CNS EC-enrichment of TCF/LEF and ZIC3 motifs in ECTS-hypo-DMRs (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This relates the protein distribution data to the RNA-seq and motif enrichment data.

claim: Among ECs, canonical Wnt signaling is largely confined to the CNS.
source: Taken together, these data imply that, among ECs, canonical Wnt signaling is largely confined to the CNS, with a corresponding restriction in the expression of TFs that mediate (LEF1) and respond to (LEF1 and ZIC3) canonical Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the Wnt reporter and TF expression data.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) was performed on 3,946 FACS-purified GFP-positive ECs from a P7 Tie2-GFP mouse brain.
source: To address these questions, we assessed EC gene expression in the developing CNS at single-cell resolution by performing single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) on 3,946 FACS-purified GFP-positive ECs from a P7 Tie2-GFP mouse brain.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) of cells revealed a single interconnected distribution of gene expression profiles suggesting a continuity of transcriptional identity across brain ECs at P7.
source: t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) of cells revealed a single interconnected distribution of gene expression profiles suggesting a continuity of transcriptional identity across brain ECs at this developmental time point consistent with the observed zonation of EC subtypes along the vasculature.
evidence: This describes the results of the t-SNE analysis.

claim: Clustering analysis identified six EC clusters that could be assigned as tip, mitotic, venous, or arterial cells (one cluster each) or capillary cells (two adjacent clusters) based on known EC subtype marker gene expression.
source: Subsequent clustering analysis identified six EC clusters (Figure 7A) that could be assigned as tip, mitotic, venous, or arterial cells (one cluster each) or capillary cells (two adjacent clusters) based on known EC subtype marker gene expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This describes the results of the clustering analysis.

claim: One of the capillary clusters is enriched for cells expressing DOPA Decarboxylase (Ddc), a gene known to be expressed in ECs in bovine aorta.
source: One of the capillary clusters is enriched for cells expressing DOPA Decarboxylase (Ddc), a gene known to be expressed in ECs in bovine aorta (Sorriento et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the expression of Ddc in one of the capillary clusters, with citation support.

claim: The ECs in the high-Ddc cluster also express multiple genes that are characteristic of arterial ECs and this cluster was therefore named 'capillary-A' (capillary-arterial).
source: The ECs in the high-Ddc cluster also express multiple genes that are characteristic of arterial ECs and this cluster was therefore named 'capillary-A' (capillary-arterial).
evidence: This describes the naming of the capillary-A cluster based on gene expression.

claim: The second capillary cluster was relatively deficient in Ddc-expressing cells, and it was enriched for cells that express genes characteristic of venous ECs.
source: The second capillary cluster was relatively deficient in Ddc-expressing cells, and it was enriched for cells that express genes characteristic of venous ECs. The second cluster was therefore named 'capillary-V' (capillary-venous).
evidence: This describes the naming of the capillary-V cluster based on gene expression.

claim: Mitotic ECs express multiple genes that are also expressed in capillary-V and venous ECs.
source: Mitotic ECs express multiple genes that are also expressed in capillary-V and venous ECs (Figure 7C), which is consistent with the observation that proliferating cells arise from veins during sprouting angiogenesis (Ehling et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014; Hasan et al., 2017; Pitulescu et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the gene expression similarity between mitotic and venous ECs, with citation support.

claim: Capillary-A ECs express multiple genes that are also expressed in tip cells and arterial ECs, but tip cells and arterial ECs show less mutual similarity.
source: Capillary-A ECs express multiple genes that are also expressed in tip cells and arterial ECs, but tip cells and arterial ECs show less mutual similarity (Figure 7C).
evidence: This describes the gene expression relationships between capillary-A, tip, and arterial ECs.

claim: The distribution of DDC was examined by immunostaining of P7 WT mouse brain.
source: The distribution of DDC was examined by immunostaining of P7 WT mouse brain (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to examine DDC distribution.

claim: DDC was localized to puncta, most likely corresponding to axon terminals of dopaminergic neurons.
source: DDC was localized to puncta, most likely corresponding to axon terminals of dopaminergic neurons; this pattern was particularly concentrated in the striatum, a brain region receiving dense dopaminergic innervation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This describes the localization of DDC in the brain.

claim: Fine- and coarse-grained heterogeneity in DDC immunostaining was detected in GS Lectin-positive capillaries in different anatomic structures within the same brain sections.
source: Most interestingly, we detected both fine- and coarse-grained heterogeneity in DDC immunostaining in GS Lectin-positive capillaries in different anatomic structures within the same brain sections, as seen by comparing the intensity of the general EC marker GS-Lectin and anti-DDC immunoreactivity.
evidence: This describes the heterogeneity of DDC expression in capillaries.

claim: Larger vessels showed minimal DDC immunoreactivity.
source: Larger vessels showed minimal DDC immunoreactivity (yellow arrows in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This describes the DDC expression in larger vessels.

claim: The heterogeneity in DDC immunoreactivity among capillary ECs likely corresponds to the differential capillary-A versus capillary-V gene expression patterns defined by scRNA-seq.
source: The heterogeneity in DDC immunoreactivity among capillary ECs likely corresponds to the differential capillary-A versus capillary-V gene expression patterns defined by scRNA-seq.
evidence: This is stated as an inference relating the immunostaining data to the scRNA-seq data.

claim: There were multiple genes expressed more or less selectively by each EC cluster.
source: Although ECs within the six clusters express many genes in common, there were multiple genes expressed more or less selectively by each cluster (Figure 7C; Supplementary file 8 lists the top 25 genes for each cluster).
evidence: This describes the differential gene expression between EC clusters.

claim: The identification of multiple new markers for tip cells substantially extends earlier screens for tip cell markers.
source: The identification of multiple new markers for tip cells is especially interesting as it substantially extends earlier screens for tip cell markers based on the overproduction of tip cells in Dll4+/- mouse retinas and on laser capture microdissection (del Toro et al., 2010; Strasser et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Five genes that were previously validated as tip cell markers in the retina — Plaur, Angpt2, Lcp2, Cxcr4, Apln, and Kcne3 — are enriched in the scRNAseq tip cell cluster.
source: Five genes that were previously validated as tip cell markers in the retina — Plaur, Angpt2, Lcp2, Cxcr4, Apln, and Kcne3 — are enriched in the scRNAseq tip cell cluster (del Toro et al., 2010; Strasser et al., 2010; Rattner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 19 of the 25 most enriched tip cell transcripts from the scRNA-seq analysis code for membrane or secreted proteins.
source: Interestingly, 19 of the 25 most enriched tip cell transcripts from the scRNA-seq analysis code for membrane or secreted proteins, many of which are known or suspected regulators of information flow.
evidence: This describes the functional categories of tip cell-enriched genes.

claim: Whole mount in situ hybridization (ISH) on P5-7 retina was performed to independently assess the expression of candidate tip cell genes.
source: To independently assess the expression of candidate tip cell genes, we performed whole mount in situ hybridization (ISH) on P5-7 retina (Figure 8).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to validate tip cell markers.

claim: Apln, Mcam, Lamb1, and Trp53i11 exhibited enriched expression at the angiogenic front of the superficial vascular plexus, indicating tip cell enrichment of these genes.
source: Consistent with the scRNA-seq analysis, Apln, Mcam, Lamb1, and Trp53i11 exhibited enriched expression at the angiogenic front of the superficial vascular plexus (Figure 8A–D), indicating tip cell enrichment of these genes.
evidence: This describes the validation of tip cell markers by ISH.

claim: Tm4sf1 exhibited only arterial expression by both scRNA-seq analysis and whole mount retina ISH.
source: As a specificity control, Tm4sf1 exhibited only arterial expression by both scRNA-seq analysis and whole mount retina ISH (Figure 8E).
evidence: This describes the validation of an arterial marker by ISH.

claim: The scRNA-seq data were used to construct a cell trajectory map.
source: To describe the relationships between the six EC clusters, the scRNA-seq data were used to construct a cell trajectory map (Figure 9A).
evidence: This describes the construction of a cell trajectory map.

claim: The cell trajectory analysis produced a map with two branch points and four terminal states [mitotic (M), venous (V), arterial (A), and tip cell (T)].
source: This analysis produced a map with two branch points and four terminal states [mitotic (M), venous (V), arterial (A), and tip cell (T)].
evidence: This describes the results of the cell trajectory analysis.

claim: Capillary-V and capillary-A ECs populate the regions adjacent to the first and second branch points, respectively.
source: Capillary-V and capillary-A ECs populate the regions adjacent to the first and second branch points, respectively.
evidence: This describes the position of capillary EC clusters in the trajectory map.

claim: The first branch point represents a choice between the venous state and the arterial and tip-cell states.
source: The first branch point represents a choice between the venous state and the arterial and tip-cell states, implying that, at the transcriptome level, tip cells are more closely related to arterial ECs than to venous ECs.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the first branch point in the trajectory map.

claim: At the transcriptome level, tip cells are more closely related to arterial ECs than to venous ECs.
source: The first branch point represents a choice between the venous state and the arterial and tip-cell states, implying that, at the transcriptome level, tip cells are more closely related to arterial ECs than to venous ECs.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the trajectory map.

claim: The second branch point represents a choice between the arterial state and the tip-cell state.
source: The second branch point represents a choice between the arterial state and the tip-cell state.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the second branch point in the trajectory map.

claim: Hey1 is more highly expressed in arterial ECs and tip cells than in venous ECs.
source: As examples of gene expression patterns that support this model, Hey1 is more highly expressed in arterial ECs and tip cells than in venous ECs, whereas Nr2f2 is more highly expressed in mitotic and venous ECs than in arterial ECs or tip-cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Hey1 across EC clusters.

claim: Nr2f2 is more highly expressed in mitotic and venous ECs than in arterial ECs or tip-cells.
source: As examples of gene expression patterns that support this model, Hey1 is more highly expressed in arterial ECs and tip cells than in venous ECs, whereas Nr2f2 is more highly expressed in mitotic and venous ECs than in arterial ECs or tip-cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Nr2f2 across EC clusters.

claim: Fbln2 and Plaur are examples of genes that are more highly expressed in arterial ECs and tip-cells, respectively.
source: Fbln2 and Plaur are examples of genes that are more highly expressed in arterial ECs and tip-cells, respectively (Figure 9B).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Fbln2 and Plaur across EC clusters.

claim: Cdkn1c/p57 expression was enriched in artery and vein ECs.
source: In particular, Cdkn1c/p57 expression was enriched in artery and vein ECs; Cdkn1a/p21 expression was enriched in mitotic cells, tip cells, and capillary-A ECs; and Cdkn2b/p15 expression was enriched in capillary-A ECs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Cdkn1c across EC clusters.

claim: Cdkn1a/p21 expression was enriched in mitotic cells, tip cells, and capillary-A ECs.
source: In particular, Cdkn1c/p57 expression was enriched in artery and vein ECs; Cdkn1a/p21 expression was enriched in mitotic cells, tip cells, and capillary-A ECs; and Cdkn2b/p15 expression was enriched in capillary-A ECs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Cdkn1a across EC clusters.

claim: Cdkn2b/p15 expression was enriched in capillary-A ECs.
source: In particular, Cdkn1c/p57 expression was enriched in artery and vein ECs; Cdkn1a/p21 expression was enriched in mitotic cells, tip cells, and capillary-A ECs; and Cdkn2b/p15 expression was enriched in capillary-A ECs (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Cdkn2b across EC clusters.

claim: Cdkn1a/p21 expression suggests that mitotic cells, tip cells, and capillary-A ECs have exited the cell cycle.
source: Cdkn1a/p21 expression suggests that these ECs have exited the cell cycle (Spencer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: TGF-beta2 (Tgfb2) was widely expressed but Latent TGF-beta-binding protein 4 (Ltbp4) expression was concentrated in arterial ECs.
source: Interestingly, TGF-beta2 (Tgfb2) was widely expressed but Latent TGF-beta-binding protein 4 (Ltbp4) expression was concentrated in arterial ECs, which utilize TGF-beta signaling to coordinate vascular smooth muscle cell development (ten Dijke and Arthur, 2007); Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Tgfb2 and Ltbp4 across EC clusters, with citation support.

claim: Transcripts coding for SMAD6 and SMAD7, two inhibitory SMADs induced by TGF-beta signaling, were enriched in the capillary-A and arterial EC clusters.
source: Transcripts coding for SMAD6 and SMAD7, two inhibitory SMADs induced by TGF-beta signaling (Afrakhte et al., 1998), were enriched in the capillary-A and arterial EC clusters (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Smad6 and Smad7 across EC clusters, with citation support.

claim: CDKN1A and CDKN2B are known to mediate TGF-beta-induced cell cycle arrest.
source: Both CDKN1A and CDKN2B are known to mediate TGF-beta-induced cell cycle arrest (Hannon and Beach, 1994; Datto et al., 1995), consistent with a role for TGF-beta signaling in CNS EC development.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Enrichment of transcripts coding for the chemokine receptor CXCR4 was observed in tip cell, capillary-A, and arterial EC clusters.
source: We also observed enrichment of transcripts coding for the chemokine receptor CXCR4 in tip cell, capillary-A, and arterial EC clusters, consistent with the role of this receptor in mediating angiogenic sprouting and artery formation (Strasser et al., 2010; Bussmann et al., 2011; Ehling et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2014; Hasan et al., 2017; Pitulescu et al., 2017); Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Cxcr4 across EC clusters, with citation support.

claim: Transcripts coding for CXCL12, the ligand for CXCR4, were highly enriched in the arterial EC cluster.
source: Transcripts coding for CXCL12, the ligand for CXCR4, were highly enriched in the arterial EC cluster, suggesting that tip cells in the developing brain vasculature may receive a CXCL12 signal from arterial ECs.
evidence: This describes the differential expression of Cxcl12 across EC clusters.

claim: CXCL12 is expressed in pulmonary and coronary arterial ECs, where it mediates patterning of arterial vasculature.
source: CXCL12 is expressed in pulmonary and coronary arterial ECs, where it mediates patterning of arterial vasculature (Chang et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.
